payload.name: wavelet-packet
payload.scope: A human-made signal decomposition method that generalizes the wavelet transform by decomposing both approximation and detail subbands at each tree level, producing a complete binary tree of subband representations. Unlike the standard wavelet transform that only recursively decomposes the approximation branch, the wavelet-packet algorithm applies the same decomposition to every node, enabling optimal basis selection for signal-specific energy concentration.

definition.body: A signal decomposition algorithm that recursively partitions a signal into subbands using a binary tree structure. At each node, both the low-frequency (approximation) and high-frequency (detail) outputs are further decomposed by a pair of quadrature mirror filters followed by downsampling. The algorithm is parameterized by: (1) the maximum decomposition depth (number of tree levels), (2) the wavelet basis function (e.g., Daubechies, Haar, Coiflet) defining the filter coefficients, (3) the node selection criteria (e.g., best-first, bottom-up, or exhaustive search over the full tree), and (4) the cost function for optimal basis selection (commonly Shannon entropy of subband energies). payload.name: gabor-transform
payload.scope: A human-made time-frequency analysis method that computes the short-time Fourier transform using a fixed Gaussian window function. Introduced by Dennis Gabor in 1946 as a 'deterministic uncertainty principle' for signal analysis, it produces a complex-valued representation of signal energy localized in both time and frequency. Unlike the general STFT where window shape and width are free parameters, the Gabor transform uses a specifically Gaussian window whose width parameter sigma controls the time-frequency resolution trade-off.

definition.body: A time-frequency representation defined by G(tau, omega) = integral from -inf to +inf of f(t) * exp(-(t-tau)^2/(2*sigma^2)) * exp(-i*omega*t) dt, where sigma is the Gaussian window width parameter controlling the time-frequency resolution trade-off. Parameters: (1) sigma — the standard deviation of the Gaussian window, determining the fixed time-frequency resolution bandwidth (Heisenberg box size = sigma * (1/(4*pi*sigma))), (2) the time and frequency sampling step sizes for discrete computation. The persistence mechanism is algorithmic and theoretical: implemented in MATLAB (gabor), Python (scipy.signal.gaussian for window generation), and image processing toolboxes; foundational to squeezed-state quantum mechanics and the Gabor frame theory of Daubechies, Grossmann, and Meyer. e.g.: MATLAB gabor function for image feature extraction; Python librosa.feature.melspectrogram using fixed Gaussian windows; Daubechies Grossmann Meyer Gabor frame theory in applied harmonic analysis textbooks | not: short-time Fourier transform with non-Gaussian window (e.g., rectangular, Hanning, Blackman windows) [formal: gaboriana transformatio | substrate: behavior | horizon: hours | explicit: yes]

payload.name: autocorrelation-method
payload.scope: A human-made signal processing method for estimating autoregressive model parameters from a finite signal segment by computing autocorrelation lags and solving the resulting Toeplitz system, producing a guaranteed-stable all-pole filter model.

definition.body: The autocorrelation method estimates autoregressive model parameters by computing autocorrelation lags of a finite-length signal segment, forming a symmetric Toeplitz system of equations, and solving for prediction coefficients that minimize the forward prediction error energy under the assumption that signal values outside the analysis window are zero. The method computes r(k) = sum_{n=0}^{N-1-k} x[n]x[n+k] for k=0..p, then solves the Toeplitz system R·a = r where R is the autocorrelation matrix. Unlike the covariance method, it pads the data with zeros outside the window, yielding a guaranteed-stable filter. Parameters: prediction order p, signal segment x[n] of length N. Persistence mechanism: standard in spectral estimation texts (e.g., Stoica Moses Spectral Analysis, Chapter 5), implemented in MATLAB's pburg as the default autocorrelation approach, embedded in spectral analysis toolkits. e.g.: computing 11th-order AR model of a 200-sample speech frame in MATLAB's aryule function; forming the autocorrelation Toeplitz matrix for spectral estimation in the Kaldi PLP pipeline; estimating AR coefficients for spectrogram inversion using zero-padded autocorrelation in Python's scipy; the covariance-based AR model in Praat speech analysis tool where the autocorrelation window is applied | not: the covariance method (uses data only within the window without zero-padding, yielding a non-Toeplitz system); the Burg method (minimizes forward and backward prediction error power with reflection coefficient constraint); Yule-Walker equations (the formalism R·a=r, not the autocorrelation data method) [formal: methodus autocorrelationis | substrate: behavior | horizon: generations | explicit: yes]
